name: Cabbage soup diet

lead: The cabbage soup diet is a short-term plan in which people eat as much low-calorie cabbage soup as they like for about seven days, with a few other foods added on set days. It is used for a fast drop in scale weight and a leaner, less bloated look.

It has circulated since at least the 1980s as a chain letter under names like Sacred Heart diet. Nutrition commentators say much of the loss in a week is water rather than fat, and that calorie intake is very low.

paras: The plan typically runs seven days, with the soup central and set foods such as fruit, vegetables or lean protein on particular days. People often use it as a short kickstart before an event or a different eating plan.
Reported side effects include fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, gas and bloating, plus possible muscle loss and nutrient shortfalls if continued. Health writers advise against long-term use.

angle.text: People use the plan for a rapid short-term drop in weight and bloating before an event. Nutrition commentators note most of a week's loss is water.

lead: The cabbage soup diet is a short-term weight-loss plan built on unlimited cabbage soup for about seven days [1]. People use it to lose scale weight quickly, reduce bloating and look leaner for an occasion.

Its origins are unclear, but it is thought to date to the 1950s and spread in the 1980s through faxed chain letters under names such as the Sacred Heart diet and the Military cabbage soup diet; the institutions named in those labels have denied any connection [1].
Popularity data show diets like this draw heavy online interest: a Google Trends analysis ranked 47 diet topics by search interest from 2004 to 2019 [2].
infobox: Sacred Heart diet; Military cabbage soup diet

paras: Dieters eat the soup freely, often as much as they want, supplemented by a few designated foods, resulting in very low calorie intake [1]. The plan promises about 10 pounds (4.5 kg) of loss in a week [1].
The diet is traced to the 1950s and was spread by photocopied and faxed chain letters in the 1980s [1]. Its institutional names have been disavowed by the organisations they reference [1].

Nutrition experts quoted in reference works say that losing that amount of body fat in a week is nearly impossible, that most loss is water and temporary, and that the calorie level is below what is considered safe long term [1].
Listed effects include dehydration, headaches, dizziness, nausea, fatigue, gas, bloating, muscle loss, brain fog and nutrient deficiencies [1].
On the T Nation forum, the diet is occasionally mentioned in discussions of fat loss and dieting history, as a past or comparison approach [3].
No studies found. A Google Trends study of diet popularity mentions diets generally rather than testing this one [2].
